L67: # COOL - Clinical Trials
L68: 
L69: At the Comparative Oral Oncology Laboratory (COOL), our research bridges discovery and clinical patient care. Through targeted clinical trials, we offer novel diagnostic and therapeutic strategies for companion animals facing oral cancers.
L70: ## Active Trial: Novel Targeted Oral Therapy for Canine Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma (OSCC)
L71: 
L72: Squamous Cell Carcinoma is the second most common oral malignancy in dogs. Because these tumors are locally invasive, rapidly erode bone, and frequently recur following conventional treatments, surgical options are sometimes limited.
L73: This study evaluates Trametinib, an FDA-approved targeted oral medication used in human oncology. Having established its safety in dogs, our goal in this expanded trial is to identify specific molecular and genetic profiles that predict favorable treatment response, allowing us to deliver precise, effective targeted therapy.
L74: 
L75: Eligibility: Dogs presented to or evaluated through the Cornell University Hospital for Animals (CUHA) with a biopsy-confirmed or strongly suspected oral squamous cell carcinoma.
L76: Financial Coverage: All diagnostic imaging, physical exams, sedation, follow-up procedures, and trial medications required during the study are provided free of charge. Additionally, dogs that complete the 126-day protocol receive an additional $1,000 credit toward standard-of-care follow-up therapy.
L77: 
L78: Owner Commitment: Administer oral medication once daily at home (chemotherapy handling and safety guidance provided).
L79: Bring your dog to CUHA for scheduled re-checks on or around Days 14, 42, 70, 108, and 126.
L80: 
L81: Complete short weekly health status surveys (via phone or in-person during visits).
L82: 
L83: Final Evaluation (Day 126): Includes a physical exam, full-body CT scan under general anesthesia to document treatment response, tumor biopsy, and fine-needle aspirates of mandibular lymph nodes for genomic analysis.
L84: 
L85: Study Leadership: Santiago Peralta, DVM, Dipl. AVDC, Founding Fellow AVDC-OMFS
L86: Sponsor: Funded by the Cornell Richard P. Riney Canine Health Center.
L87: 
L88: How to Enroll or Refer a Patient: If you are a dog owner interested in screening, or a veterinarian seeking to refer a patient for trial evaluation:

L31: Mission
L32: ## Designer cell therapies for pets first — and their people next.
L33: 
L34: When a pet gets sick, families face limited options. LEAH Labs is changing that. We combine world-class gene editing with novel protein engineering to revolutionize companion animal oncology — while generating the insights that will power the next generation of human CAR-T therapies.
L35: 
L36: > Translational medicine is in our DNA.
L37: 
L38: 1st ever
L39: We're the first, and only, in the world to put pets in remissions using CAR-T cell therapy in dogs with cancer.
L40: 
L41: The only CAR-T cell therapy company for dogs
L42: 
L43: World leading vets are testing CAR-T cells in pets, but we're the only ones doing this commercially.
L44: 
L45: Our trials are fully funded
L46: 
L47: We cover 100% of the costs for pet parents who enroll in our trials
L48: 
L49: Science
L50: ## Purpose built for pets.
L51: Advanced enough for humans.
L52: 
L53: Four pillars. One platform.
L54: 
L55: 01
L56: 
L57: ### Generative Biology & De Novo Protein Engineering
L58: 
L59: Leveraging breakthroughs in AI and protein design, LEAH Labs designs, builds, and tests novel therapeutic assets that didn't evolve in nature. We're not iterating on legacy biology — we're inventing new biology from first principles.
L60: 
L61: 02
L62: ### Precision Gene Editing — GeneWeld
L63: 
L64: Our founder invented our gene editing platform during their PhD. This platform is a critical enabling technology that allows us to build CAR-T cell therapies at costs affordable to pet parents.
L65: 
L66: 03
L67: ### Harnessing Immune Cells to Fight Cancer
L68: 
L69: The immune system can detect and destroy cancer — but cancer evades it. Gene editing lets us reprogram T cells to become professional cancer-fighting assassins. CAR-T cell therapy is already curative in human blood cancers. We're bringing it their furry family members.
L70: 
L71: 04
L72: ### Canine Translational Oncology
L73: 
L74: Dogs develop the same spontaneous cancers as humans, in a shared environment, with a fully intact immune system. Disease in dogs mirrors disease in people. Every remission in a dog is a data point that accelerates human medicine — compressing timelines that would otherwise take a decade.
L75: 
L76: Clinical Trial
L77: ## Our next clinical trial launches in May 2026
L78: 
L79: Our fully-funded clinical trial will be enrolling dogs diagnosed with B cell lymphoma. If you can travel to one of our three partner institutions, we want to hear from you. Treatment is provided at no cost to enrolled families.
L80:

L20: Clinical trials and collaborative research in surgical oncology are actively encouraged by the VSSO. Prospective clinical trials are preferred, but multi-institutional retrospective case series will also be strongly considered. Research projects can include, but are not limited to, the study of new surgical techniques, multimodality treatment protocols, novel adjuvant agents, and treatment outcomes for different tumor types.

L41: # JUNE 2026
L42: 
L43: Evaluation of incidence and risk factors for surgical site infection following neoplastic canine limb amputations performed with and without a bipolar sealing device
L44: 
L45: Lead investigator: Andrea Erickson, DVM, DACVS-SA, ACVS Fellow – Surgical Oncology, EDUCT-MA (BME), Assistant Professor – Surgical Oncology and Soft Tissue Surgery, Oregon State University
L46: 
L47: Aim and objectives:
L48: The aim of this study is to evaluate the incidence and risk factors for surgical site infection (SSI) following neoplastic limb amputations performed with and without a bipolar vessel sealing device. Furthermore, we want to evaluate the influence of anesthetic and surgical time on SSI incidence for neoplastic limb amputations.
L49: 
L50: Please contact Dr. Erickson (erickand@oregonstate.edu) for more details.

L53: # OCTOBER 2025
L54: 
L55: Retrospective evaluation of impact of lymphadenectomy on survival of dogs with cutaneous mast cell tumors.
L56: 
L57: Lead investigator: Dr. Mirja Nolff (Clinic of Small Animal Surgery, Vetsuisse Zürich, University of Zürich, Switzerland).
L58: 
L59: Aim and objectives:
L60: The aim of this study is, to assess the impact of nodal management on outcome in dogs with grade 2/low grade mast cell tumors that are solely treated by surgical intervention. Furthermore, we want to assess if SLN based resection results in a superior outcome compared to regional lymphadenectomy. Our hypothesis is, that lymphadenectomy will result in improved survival time compared to cases were lymph-nodes were not treated in both species.
L61: Furthermore, we propose that this effect will be more pronounced in dogs when SLN mapping was used to determine the nodes to be resected.
L62: Please contact Dr. Nolff (mnolff@vetclinics.uzh.ch) for more details.

L65: # 2022
L66: ## The effects of lymph node extirpation on long-term prognosis of non-metastatic canine oral malignant melanoma.
L67: 
L68: Lead investigator: Dr. Judith Bertran
L69: 
L70: Aims and objectives of the study:
L71: 
L72:   1. To compare the disease progression rates, survival times of two treatment groups of nonmetastatic canine oral malignant melanoma (Stage I and Stage II with N0)— (1) primary tumor/local surgical excision (group 1) versus (2) primary tumor removal with non-selective cervical LNs extirpation (group 2).
L73:   2. To determine complications related to non-selective lymph node extirpation of the cervical
L74: 
L75: lymph nodes (> or = of 3 LNs).
L76: 
L77:   3. To evaluate the disease progression rate and survival times of a subgroup of dogs with OMM Stage I or II (with N0) that undergo a non-metastatic sentinel LN removal only.
